title: Week 111 · Lesson 135: Pediatric Ear, Nose & Throat Disorders — FNP-Level Diagnosis, Stewardship and Airway Safety
html:
PHASE 5 · FAMILY & LIFESPAN PRIMARY CARE

Week 111 — Lesson 135: Pediatric Ear, Nose & Throat Disorders

FNP-level goal: Distinguish viral upper-respiratory illness from acute otitis media, otitis externa, streptococcal pharyngitis, bacterial sinusitis, deep-neck infection, and airway emergency; use examination and testing precisely; practice antimicrobial stewardship; and provide a reliable follow-up and escalation plan.

Learning Objectives

  • Diagnose acute otitis media using middle-ear effusion and tympanic-membrane findings rather than redness alone.
  • Differentiate AOM, otitis media with effusion, otitis externa, and mastoid complications.
  • Use age and viral features to guide group A streptococcal testing and confirm negative rapid tests when indicated.
  • Recognize persistent, worsening, and severe-onset patterns of acute bacterial sinusitis.
  • Identify drooling, trismus, neck swelling, toxic appearance, orbital findings, and respiratory distress as urgent red flags.

Part 1 — Begin With Airway and Hydration

Most pediatric ENT complaints are self-limited, but the same chief complaint can hide airway obstruction or invasive infection. Before looking at the ear or throat, assess voice, cry, secretion handling, breathing, position, color, mental status, perfusion, and ability to drink. Drooling, tripod position, stridor, muffled voice with distress, severe trismus, neck swelling, cyanosis, or toxic appearance requires urgent or emergency evaluation.

Do not force an agitated child with suspected upper-airway obstruction to lie down for a complete throat examination. Protecting the airway takes priority over confirming the office diagnosis.

Part 2 — Ear Pain Is a Differential

Ear pain may arise from AOM, otitis externa, foreign body, trauma, pressure injury, cerumen, temporomandibular disease, dental pathology, or referred throat pain. Ask onset, fever, URI symptoms, drainage, swimming, instrumentation, hearing change, prior infections, tubes, antibiotic exposure, immune status, and pain behind the ear.

Inspect the pinna and canal before the tympanic membrane. Tragal or pinna tenderness and canal inflammation support otitis externa; middle-ear disease requires assessment beyond canal findings.

Part 3 — Acute Otitis Media Requires Effusion

AOM is supported by moderate-to-severe tympanic-membrane bulging or new otorrhea not caused by otitis externa. Mild bulging plus recent otalgia or intense erythema can also support diagnosis. A red tympanic membrane alone is nonspecific because crying, fever, or instrumentation can cause erythema.

Use pneumatic otoscopy or tympanometry when feasible to identify middle-ear effusion. Remove obstructing cerumen safely. Document laterality, bulging, mobility, effusion, otorrhea, and severity rather than writing only “red ear.”

Part 4 — AOM Treatment Is Age and Severity Dependent

Assess pain for every child and provide age-appropriate analgesia. Antibiotic versus observation decisions depend on age, laterality, severity, diagnostic certainty, recent antibiotic exposure, allergy, concurrent purulent conjunctivitis, recurrence, comorbidity, and follow-up reliability. Severe otalgia, prolonged pain, high fever, or specific young-child bilateral disease patterns favor treatment.

When observation is appropriate, it is an active plan: the family must have access to reassessment and a mechanism to start therapy if symptoms worsen or fail to improve within 48–72 hours. When antibiotics are indicated, follow current pediatric dosing, allergy assessment, recent exposure, and local resistance guidance. Reassess treatment failure rather than automatically extending the same drug.

Part 5 — Otitis Media With Effusion

OME is middle-ear fluid without acute infection findings. It may follow AOM or occur with eustachian-tube dysfunction. Antibiotics do not routinely clear sterile effusion. Ask about hearing, speech, learning, balance, recurrent disease, craniofacial conditions, and developmental risk.

Persistent effusion with hearing concern, speech delay, school difficulty, structural abnormality, or high-risk developmental status requires hearing evaluation and possible ENT referral. A normal pain level does not make chronic hearing impact unimportant.

Part 6 — Otitis Externa

Otitis externa is suggested by canal pain, tragal or pinna tenderness, edema, erythema, debris, and swimming or instrumentation history. Assess whether the tympanic membrane is intact because this affects safe topical selection. Avoid unnecessary systemic antibiotics for uncomplicated localized disease.

Severe pain out of proportion, cranial-nerve findings, spreading cellulitis, fever with systemic illness, diabetes, or immune compromise raises concern for invasive disease and requires urgent specialty or emergency evaluation.

Part 7 — Mastoid and Foreign-Body Safety

Postauricular erythema, swelling, tenderness, protrusion of the auricle, persistent fever, severe headache, or toxic appearance may indicate mastoiditis or another complication. Arrange urgent imaging and specialty evaluation rather than prescribing another routine outpatient course.

For ear foreign bodies, consider object type, location, cooperation, and prior attempts. Button batteries require immediate removal because caustic injury progresses rapidly. Stop repeated attempts when trauma or deeper impaction is likely and obtain ENT support.

Part 8 — Pharyngitis: Viral or Group A Strep?

GAS pharyngitis is most common from ages 5–15 and is rare as classic acute pharyngitis under age three. Sudden sore throat, fever, tender anterior cervical nodes, palatal petechiae, and tonsillar inflammation increase suspicion. Cough, rhinorrhea, hoarseness, oral ulcers, and conjunctivitis strongly support viral infection and generally make GAS testing unnecessary.

Clinical findings alone cannot reliably confirm GAS when viral features are absent. Use a rapid antigen or molecular strategy according to current guidance. For symptomatic children age three and older, CDC recommends confirming a negative rapid antigen test with throat culture unless a validated molecular approach or local protocol provides equivalent sensitivity. Treat confirmed infection; avoid antibiotics for a negative culture.

Part 9 — Complicated Sore Throat

Peritonsillar abscess may cause unilateral severe pain, muffled voice, trismus, uvular deviation, drooling, and reduced intake. Retropharyngeal infection may produce fever, neck stiffness, swelling, torticollis, or respiratory symptoms, especially in younger children. Epiglottitis is less common after vaccination but remains an airway emergency.

Airway symptoms, toxic appearance, deep-neck swelling, inability to swallow secretions, dehydration, or neurologic complication warrants emergency evaluation. Do not delay for an office throat swab.

Part 10 — Sinusitis Is a Clinical Time Pattern

Colored nasal discharge alone does not diagnose bacterial sinusitis. AAP criteria support acute bacterial sinusitis when URI symptoms persist more than 10 days without improvement, worsen after initial improvement, or begin severely with high fever and purulent discharge for at least three consecutive days. Sequential viral infections can mimic persistence, so clarify the timeline carefully.

Routine imaging is not recommended for uncomplicated sinusitis. Orbital swelling, impaired eye movement, proptosis, visual change, severe frontal headache, altered mental status, meningeal signs, or focal neurologic findings require urgent imaging, hospital care, and specialty consultation for orbital or intracranial complication.

Part 11 — Antibiotic Stewardship

An antibiotic decision requires a defensible diagnosis, indication, agent, dose, duration, allergy assessment, and reassessment plan. Avoid treating viral URI, isolated tympanic erythema, OME, or a positive strep test in a child whose syndrome is clearly viral without considering carrier status.

Ask what happened with the reported allergy. Many labels reflect intolerance or an old rash rather than immediate hypersensitivity; accurate evaluation improves future treatment. Counsel caregivers that antibiotic adverse effects and resistance are real harms.

Part 12 — Prevention and Longitudinal Care

Review influenza, COVID-19, pneumococcal, Hib, and routine vaccines; smoke exposure; hand hygiene; swimming and ear instrumentation; dental health; allergic rhinitis; and sleep-disordered breathing. Recurrent snoring, witnessed apnea, daytime dysfunction, or adenotonsillar hypertrophy requires focused sleep evaluation rather than repeated infection treatment.

Clinical Case 1 — The Red Ear Trap

A crying 18-month-old has URI symptoms and a red but nonbulging, mobile tympanic membrane without effusion. The FNP does not label AOM, treats discomfort and viral symptoms, and provides follow-up if pain or fever worsens.

Clinical Case 2 — Negative Rapid Test

An eight-year-old has sudden sore throat, fever, tender anterior cervical nodes, no cough, and a negative rapid antigen test. The FNP sends the recommended backup throat culture and withholds antibiotics unless confirmation is positive, while giving hydration and emergency precautions.

Clinical Case 3 — Eye Swelling Changes the Disposition

A ten-year-old with worsening sinus symptoms develops eyelid swelling, pain with eye movement, fever, and headache. The FNP sends the child for emergency evaluation of orbital complication rather than ordering routine outpatient antibiotics alone.

FNP High-Yield Framework: ENT SAFE

  1. E — Evaluate airway: voice, drooling, stridor, trismus, neck swelling, hydration.
  2. N — Name the anatomy: canal, middle ear, pharynx, sinus, deep neck.
  3. T — Test only when indicated: effusion-based AOM, age-appropriate GAS confirmation, no routine sinus imaging.
  4. S — Stratify severity: age, laterality, pain, fever, immune risk, complications.
  5. A — Apply stewardship: correct diagnosis, targeted drug, allergy history, reassessment.
  6. F — Follow the loop: observation mechanism, culture result, hearing or ENT referral.
  7. E — Escalate danger: airway compromise, mastoid, orbital, intracranial, deep-neck findings.

Take-Home Summary

ENT care rewards diagnostic precision. AOM requires middle-ear effusion and characteristic membrane findings; GAS testing follows age and symptom pattern; bacterial sinusitis follows duration and trajectory; and airway, mastoid, orbital, or deep-neck complications change the encounter from routine primary care to urgent evaluation.

Educational note: Use current AAP, CDC, local antimicrobial, allergy, and emergency guidance. Drooling with distress, stridor, cyanosis, deep-neck swelling, severe trismus, mastoid findings, orbital symptoms, focal neurologic change, or inability to hydrate requires urgent care.
